deep.reconstruction:
Setting. Let I = ]0, ω[ with 0 < ω ≤ +∞, carrying Lebesgue measure. K^∞(I) denotes the bounded measurable functions with compact support. K^∞_K(K) denotes those supported in a compact K. The previous page introduced the decreasing rearrangement φ_f of a real function f and the Hardy–Littlewood inequality ∫ fg ≤ ∫ φ_f φ_g (Prop. 2). The heading says 'Fonctions de Weyl', but the object defined here is what the next page renames a 'fonction de Pólya'.

Definition 1. A real function P on K^∞(I) is required to satisfy three conditions.
(P1) Rearrangement invariance: P(f) = P(g) whenever f and g are equimeasurable, i.e. have the same distribution function, equivalently φ_f = φ_g.
(P2) Convexity.
(P3) Sequential lower semicontinuity: for every compact K and every sequence f_i in K^∞_K(K) converging in measure to f, P(f) ≤ liminf P(f_i). The proof shows a bounded sequence is meant.

Claim. P3 is equivalent to the apparently weaker condition P3': for each compact K, the restriction of P to L^∞(K) is lower semicontinuous for the weak* topology σ(L^∞(K), L^1(K)).

P3' ⇒ P3: a bounded sequence converging in measure on a finite-measure set converges weak* (dominated convergence).

P3 ⇒ P3': fix a and let A = {f ∈ L^∞(K) : P(f) ≤ a}.
- A is convex by P2, and closed under limits in measure of bounded sequences by P3.
- By Banach–Dieudonné (Krein–Šmulian), A is weak* closed as soon as its intersection with every ball of L^∞(K) is weak* closed.
- Such an intersection is convex, bounded, and closed in the L^1(K) norm (L^1 convergence gives a.e.-convergent subsequences, hence convergence in measure). It is therefore σ(L^1, L^∞)-closed.
- On bounded subsets of L^∞(K), σ(L^∞, L^1) coincides with the topology induced by σ(L^1, L^∞), since L^∞ is dense in L^1. Hence the intersection is weak* closed.

What the page serves (next page). Using Hahn–Banach / Fenchel duality, symmetrization of affine minorants via Prop. 2, and weak* lsc, a Pólya function is a supremum of affine functionals a_i + ∫ φ_i φ_f with φ_i decreasing. This is a continuous Hardy–Littlewood–Pólya majorization duality. A 'Weyl function' W on positive functions is then one for which W(exp f) is a Pólya function, so W(f) = sup_i (a_i + ∫ φ_i log φ_f). This is the continuous analogue of Weyl's 1949 theorem: if Φ(e^t) is convex, then Σ Φ(|λ_i|) ≤ Σ Φ(s_i), i.e. log-majorization. Pólya's 1950 remark reduced Weyl's theorem to majorization. The aim is evidently eigenvalue / singular-value inequalities for operators, in the 1953–56 Fredholm-theory / tensor-product context.
errors: P3 as written ('toute suite (f_i) dans K^∞_K(K) tendant ... en mesure') imposes no uniform bound. Without one, P3 is strictly stronger than P3' and the claimed equivalence fails. Counterexample: P(f) = -∫f is linear, rearrangement-invariant and weak*-continuous. Take f_i = i·1_{]0,1/i[}, which tends to 0 in measure, with P(f_i) = -1 < 0 = P(0). The proof itself only uses bounded sequences, and a crossed phrase seems to have contained 'bornée', so 'suite bornée' should be restored in P3.
The direction P3 ⇒ P3' uses P2 (convexity) essentially, via Krein–Šmulian and Mazur. The equivalence is therefore an equivalence within the class of convex functions, which the text only implies.

Terminological instability: here the heading calls the object a 'fonction de Weyl', while on the next page the same axioms define a 'fonction de Pólya'. 'Weyl' is reserved there for W with W∘exp Pólya.

ideas.what: Axiomatization of convex, rearrangement-invariant, lsc functionals on bounded functions on ]0, ω[, ω ≤ ∞
ideas.modern_name: Rearrangement-invariant (symmetric) convex functionals; continuous Schur-convex functions; Orlicz/Lorentz-type modulars
ideas.usually_credited_to: Hardy–Littlewood–Pólya (discrete, 1929/1934); continuous theory: G.G. Lorentz (1950s), Ryff (1965), Luxemburg (1967), Chong (1974)
ideas.where_published: Possibly related material in Produits tensoriels topologiques (1955) / La théorie de Fredholm (1956) on eigenvalue inequalities; not verified

ideas.what: Equivalence of sequential lsc in measure (bounded sequences) with weak* lsc for convex functionals, proved via Banach–Dieudonné
ideas.modern_name: Krein–Šmulian argument; convex sets closed in measure are weak* closed
ideas.where_published: Grothendieck used Banach–Dieudonné heavily (Espaces vectoriels topologiques, São Paulo 1954), but this specific application is not known to me

ideas.what: (next page, prepared here) Representation of such functionals as sup of a_i + ∫ φ_i φ_f with φ_i decreasing, and 'Weyl functions' W with W∘exp of Pólya type
ideas.modern_name: Continuous majorization duality; log-majorization / continuous Weyl majorant theorem
ideas.usually_credited_to: Weyl (1949), Pólya (1950) discrete; continuous / von Neumann algebra form: Fack (1982), Fack–Kosaki (1986)

missed.claim: Grothendieck sets up majorization and Weyl log-majorization on an interval ]0, ω[ with 0 < ω ≤ +∞, using decreasing rearrangements and weak* lsc. This is exactly the framework later used for generalized singular values μ_t(T) of τ-measurable operators in semifinite von Neumann algebras, where ω = τ(1). There, continuous Weyl inequalities ∫ f(μ_t(AB)) ≤ ∫ f(μ_t(A) μ_t(B)) (Fack 1982, Fack–Kosaki 1986) play the role of his 'Weyl functions'. The 1953 notes appear to anticipate a continuous Weyl-majorization formalism decades earlier; whether he applied it to operators is not visible on this page.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical priority for the continuous (non-discrete) Weyl/Pólya majorization theory underlying symmetric operator spaces and noncommutative Lp / Orlicz theory. Probably an unpublished precursor rather than new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is standard by modern standards: rearrangement-invariant convex functionals, and a Krein–Šmulian closure argument with a minor gap about boundedness. It is a mild historical curiosity that in 1953 Grothendieck had an axiomatic continuous version of Weyl/Pólya majorization on ]0, ω], ω ≤ ∞. This predates Ryff, Luxemburg and Fack–Kosaki, but it is not a new result today.
transcription_corrections: 'sont spectralement[?] équivalentes' is more likely 'sont équimesurables' (or 'également réparties'), matching the previous page's terminology; the word is hard to read.
In P3, the crossed phrase after 'tendant' seems to include 'une suite bornée'. The intended condition is a bounded sequence converging in measure to a limit f, rather than 'tendant simplement'.
'fermé pour la convergence dans L^∞(K) pour la convergence en mesure' should read roughly 'fermé pour les suites bornées dans L^∞(K) qui convergent en mesure'.

The sentence beginning 'Or on sait aussi que A est déjà faiblement fermé' reads more plausibly: 'Or on sait que pour que A soit faiblement fermé, il suffit, en vertu du th. de Banach–Dieudonné, ... que son intersection avec toute partie bornée de L^∞(K) le soit'. One then reduces to A bounded in L^∞(K), hence contained in L^1(K) and closed there for the strong topology.
Margin at top left: 'K^∞, L^∞_K(K)' with a crossed note and 'K^∞_K' below; these are notation reminders.
'Soit M ...' and 'sur H' are crossed-out remnants (probably 'sur M', the measure space of the previous section).
